For its proposed capital structure and Return on Equity (ROE)\Weighted 
Average Cost of Capital (WACC) proposals, the Company relied on the testimony of its 
consultant, Mr. Vincent Rea. Mr. Rea developed a recommendation, adopted by 
Eversource and presented to the Commission for its approval, for an ROE (cost of 
common equity) for the Company of 10.80 percent, based on a “reasonable range” of 
10.30 to 11.30 percent. Mr. Rea developed his cost of equity recommendation by 
referring to the Discounted Cash Flow model approach, a Capital Asset Pricing Model, 
an Empirical Capital Asset Pricing Model, and a Risk Premium Model. The Company 
stated that it elected to seek an ROE of 10.30 percent, elaborating that “…the 
Company has elected to propose a cost of equity in this proceeding of 10.30 percent, 
which falls at the lower-end of the range of reasonableness…[t]he Company’s proposed 
ROE in this proceeding represents a conservative estimate of its cost of equity in the 
current capital markets environment, and should, therefore, be approved by the

DE 24-070 
- 11 - 
 
 
 
Commission.” Docket Tab #284 at 39; Hearing Exhibit 9 at Bates Pages 19,350; 
19,363; 19,375; 19,389 through 19,390. 
 
Mr. Rea also evaluated the reasonableness of the Company’s proposed capital 
structure by comparing it to the capital structure ratios of the “electric utility proxy 
group,” comprised of a group of publicly traded utility companies with risk 
characteristics similar to the Company, based on permanent capitalization, which 
excludes short-term debt. Hearing Exhibit 9, Bates Page 19,386. On this basis, the 
Company proposed a rate-setting capital structure consisting of 53.85 percent 
common equity and 46.15 percent long-term debt, which produces a WACC figure of 
7.44 percent applied to the Company’s proposed rate case accounting. Hearing Exhibit 
9, at Bates Pages 19,385 through 19,386; 19,303.

In considering the question of ROE9, the Commission must assess whether the 
ROE that is set as a rate of return for used and useful investments by the Company is 
sufficient to assure investor confidence in the financial soundness of the utility, and 
enough to maintain and support its credit so that it will be able to raise the funding 
necessary to improve and expand its service to customers. New England Tel. & Tel. Co. 
v. State, 104 N.H. 229, 234 (1962). The Commission must also set this reasonable rate 
of return while giving appropriately due recognition to the competing interests of the 
Company and its investors on the one hand, and of the customers who pay the rates 
established on the other, in keeping with the Commission’s role as arbiter. The 
Commission should set a rate sufficient to yield a return comparable “to that generally 
made at the same time and in the same general part of the country on investments in 
other business undertakings which are attended by corresponding risks and 
uncertainties.” Appeal of Conservation Law Foundation of New England, Inc., 127 N.H. 
606, 635-636 (1986), citing Bluefield Co. v. Pub. Serv. Comm., 262 U.S. 679, 692 
(1923), and New England Tel. & Tel. Co., 104 N.H. at 234 (other citations omitted); RSA 
363:17-a. On the other hand, the actual needs of the Company do not control what 
the Commission may do when it sets the rate of return and the other variables that 
determine allowable revenue. The Commission may set the “sufficient” rate of return 
by reference to a capital structure that it finds appropriate, rather than the actual 
capital structure of the Company. Appeal of Conservation Law Foundation, 127 N.H. at 
 
9 The Commission acknowledges the parties’ citations to the federal Hope and Bluefield standards as 
relating to ROE, but insofar as the New Hampshire Constitution is at least as protective of the Company’s 
constitutional rights against takings as the U.S. Constitution, see State v. Ball, 124 N.H. 226, 231-234 
(1983), the Commission shall rely on New Hampshire legal standards and precedent in rendering its 
decisions here.

DE 24-070 
- 41 - 
 
 
 
635-636, citing New England Tel. & Tel. Co., 104 N.H. at 236 (other citations omitted). 
The Commission has authority to set the rate of return by reference to appropriate, as 
distinguished from actual, capital structure because the object of the process is to 
strike a fair balance between recognizing the interests of the customer and those of the 
investor. Appeal of Conservation Law Foundation, 127 N.H. at 636, citing Power 
Comm’n v. Hope Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591, 603 (1944) and Chicopee Mfg. Co. v. Public 
Service Co., 98 N.H. 5, 11 (1953). The Commission can allow a rate of return in excess 
of the utility’s cost of capital (cost of money); how much more than the cost of capital 
“shall be allowed” for a rate of return to a public utility depends upon the 
Commission’s determination as to what is a just and reasonable return. Chicopee Mfg. 
Co., 98 N.H. at 12-13, citing New England Tel. & Tel. Co. v. State, 95 N.H. 353, 361 
(1949). Thus, it is realistic to stress the role that the Commission’s judgment must 
play in setting a sufficient and reasonable rate of return for the Company. Appeal of 
Conservation Law Foundation, 127 N.H. at 636, citing Bluefield Co. v. Pub. Serv. 
Comm., 262 U.S. at 692 (other citations omitted). 
 
In this case, having reviewed the record before us, and the arguments of the 
parties related thereto on these issues, we find the recommendations of Dr. Woolridge, 
submitted on behalf of the DOE, Hearing Exhibit 16, as augmented by his oral 
testimony, compelling, and hereby adopt them concerning the ROE figure of 9.50 
percent, the recommended capital ratio of 50 percent debt to 50 percent Common 
Equity, and the resultant weighted average cost of capital figure for Eversource of 6.80 
percent. See Hearing Exhibit 16 at Bates Page 11. Dr. Woolridge is a subject-matter 
expert on ROE that has contributed analyses to several Commission rate proceedings. 
See, e.g., Docket No. DE 19-057, Hearing Exhibit 36; see also Hearing Exhibit 16 at

DE 24-070 
- 42 - 
 
 
 
Bates Pages 137-138. We are persuaded by Dr. Woolridge’s testimony and analysis, 
including his critiques of the Company’s witnesses, and find that his 
recommendations for the Company’s return on equity, capital ratio, and weighted 
average cost of capital will result in just and reasonable rates. Dr. Woolridge presents 
his recommendations as a fair compromise between the needs of the Company for a 
capital-attractive rate of return, the need to ameliorate financial risks associated with 
debt, and associated costs, Hearing Exhibit 16 at Bates Page 38-41, and the interests 
of customers in avoiding rate shock. As presented, Dr. Woolridge’s proxy analyses, 
offer a reasonable approach that conforms with the New Hampshire legal standards 
governing comparability of earnings, and we adopt them. Appeal of Conservation Law 
Foundation of New England, Inc., 127 N.H. 606, 635-636 (1986), citing Bluefield Co. v. 
Pub. Serv. Comm., 262 U.S. 679, 692 (1923), and New England Tel. & Tel. Co., 104 
N.H. at 234. 
 
As shown in the graphic presented in Ms. Perry’s testimony, filed on behalf of 
Wal-Mart, Inc., Hearing Exhibit 34 at Bates Page 13, the 9.5 percent ROE level is well 
within the range of comparability among investor-owned utilities in the Northeastern 
United States. Furthermore, this ROE is in line with that approved by the Commission 
recently for Eversource’s New Hampshire investor-owned utility peers: Unitil Electric 
Systems, Inc. (Order No. 26,623 (May 3, 2022); 9.2 percent ROE, 7.42 percent WACC); 
and Liberty Utilities (Granite State Electric) d/b/a Liberty (Order No. 28,135 (April 24, 
2025), and Order No. 26,376 (June 30, 2020); 9.1 percent ROE, 7.708 WACC).  
 
We find that a 9.5 percent ROE is comparable to the returns on equity enjoyed 
by the Company’s peers, and will allow the Company to attract capital investment; the 
50-50 capital-to-debt ratio will serve to control debt-incurred financial risk and serves

DE 24-070 
- 43 - 
 
 
 
to reduce the financial burden on Eversource’s customers, as compared with the 
Company’s original proposals. After considering all the evidence presented in this 
case, we find that the DOE’s recommended ROE, capital-to-debt ratio, and resulting 
WACC calculation for the Company are just and reasonable and produce just and 
reasonable rates. We therefore ADOPT and INCORPORATE into our alternative 
regulation of the Company’s distribution rates the DOE’s recommendations for the 
Company’s ROE, capital-to-debt ratio, and resulting WACC calculation.  
 
In doing so, we are not persuaded by the OCA’s argument and expert testimony, 
Hearing Exhibits 22 and 24, that a much lower 8.13 percent ROE would still allow the 
Company to realize a reasonable return or continue to attract investment capital. 
Instead, we find that the OCA proposed ROE was neither just nor reasonable, nor 
would it result in just and reasonable rates. Thus, we REJECT OCA’s proposed ROE in 
favor of the DOE’s recommended ROE. 
 
Likewise, we did not find the Company’s arguments in favor of the 10.3 ROE 
proposal persuasive. The Company’s use of non-regulated companies in its proxy 
analysis, as criticized by Dr. Woolridge, did not give the Commission confidence 
regarding the reasonableness of its analysis, nor do we accept the Company’s over-
optimistic growth forecasts, and over-stated market risk premiums, applied in Mr. 
Rea’s analyses. See Hearing Exhibit 16 at Bates Pages 94-136.

4 The ESM credits customers with a 75% share of ROE beyond a 25-basis point threshold (.25%) on the

on the full year prior 2025. The impact of this adjustment would be excluded in calculating the

The parties and intervenors rejected the Company's stated need for alternative 
ratemaking, with the partial exception of CLF, which recommended a “stakeholder 
process” to evaluate the mechanism and develop appropriate performance metrics. 
The DOE and the OCA advocated for significantly lower ROE: the OCA recommended 
an 8.13 percent ROE, while the DOE recommended 9.50 percent ROE. The OCA, 
AARP, and Ms. Kramer all advocated for a lower fixed customer charge than that 
proposed by the Company (as discussed below). Furthermore, in the testimonial 
presentations of its witnesses, including the DOE’s consultant, Ms. Donna Mullinax, 
see e.g., Hearing Exhibit 41, the DOE recommended a series of Adjustments to reflect 
recommended disallowances to the Company’s rate-base and O&M accounting, as 
discussed below.

For the various reasons delineated below, the Commission has determined to 
adopt some aspects of the DOE’s recommendations related to adjustments for the 
Company’s proposals regarding rate base, O&M expense, ROE, and Eversource’s 
capital ratio. The Commission carefully considered all the parties' inputs, but applied 
the DOE’s methodology. Notably, the analysis in this section includes the final 
Eversource permanent rate request of $102.8 million, originally $182 million, and 
does not include the $35 million PBR request.

C. 
Cost of Capital and Capital Structure  
 
Expert testimony offered by Versant’s expert consultant, Staff’s expert consultant, 
and the OPA’s expert recommended a range of returns on equity (ROE) and different 
capital structures. The Commission concludes that a ROE of 9.35% and a capital 
structure consisting of 3.35% short-term debt, 46.62% long-term debt, 0.03% preferred 
stock, and 50.00% common equity will provide Versant’s investors the opportunity to 
earn a fair return on their investment. 
 
1. 
Versant’s Proposal 
 
Notwithstanding that John Trogonoski, Versant’s ROE expert, recommends 
increasing the ROE to a range from 10.33% to 10.78%, Versant proposes to maintain its 
allowed ROE of 9.35% to help mitigate the impact of the rate increase on customers. 
Reply Brief at 38. Versant, however, proposes to change the percentage of equity 
included in its capital structure from 49% to 50% (Exhibit RR-2), which it states more 
accurately reflects Versant’s actual capital structure, as Versant’s actual equity 
percentage has been approximately 51% during 2022 and 2023. Versant claims that its 
actual earned ROE has been lower than its allowed ROE for the last several years as 
shown in Versant’s 2022 annual report to the Commission, with Versant earning only 
3.50% in 2022. See Versant Rev. Req. Test. at 10-11; see also Versant Brief at 41. 
Versant argues that a ROE below 9.35% would not be reasonable and would result in 
unjust and unreasonable rates. Versant Brief at 39. 
 
In its Reply Brief, Versant repeats its agreement with and recommendation of 
Staff’s expert that the Commission approve a capital structure of 50% equity and a ROE 
of 9.35%. Versant Reply Brief at 40; 42.

Order  
 
                                      27                        Docket No. 2023-00336 
 
 
 
2. 
Parties’ Positions 
 
The OPA recommends that the Commission use a two-stage discounted cash 
flow (DCF) in calculating Versant’s cost of equity in this proceeding as presented by its 
cost of capital expert witness, Mr. Houck. Mr. Houck recommends reliance on this model 
even though the Commission traditionally uses the constant growth model, also known 
as a single stage, DCF modeling approach in determining the allowed cost of equity for 
Maine utilities in general rate proceedings. Mr. Houck contends that the single stage 
model tends to overstate a utility’s cost of equity due to upward biases extrapolating 
earnings growth that are embedded in that methodology. Consequently, the OPA 
suggests that the Commission recognize those issues and adopt Mr. Houck’s estimate 
of Versant’s cost of equity of 9.09%. June 15, 2024 Houck Test. at 24:1-8; OPA Brief at 
15, 18. 
 
The OPA further recommends that the Commission use the capital structure of 
ENMAX in calculating Versant’s overall cost of capital, reducing the common equity 
component of Versant’s capital structure for ratemaking purposes from around 50% to 
around 47%. Additionally, the OPA suggests that such an adjustment is needed because 
ENMAX used a significant amount of debt to purchase Versant’s equity.35  
 
3. 
Staff’s Position 
 
Dr. Randall Woolridge, Staff’s expert, recommends in his surrebuttal testimony, a 
9.15% ROE (see Reply B.A. at 11) in conjunction with a 50% capitalization ratio for 
common equity. Reply B.A, Ex. 2 at 31. However, at the December Hearing, Dr. 
Woolridge acknowledged that, given changes in the capital markets, if he were to make 
a recommendation on that day, he would return to his original recommendation of 
9.35% ROE on common equity. Dec. 19, 2024 Hr’g Tr. at 30:14-21; see also B.A., Ex. 2 
at 5:3.  
 
 
 
35 Specifically, as described in the Versant’s response to OPA-002-015, two of the four 
series of debt used to acquire Versant Power remain outstanding: (1) a $300 million 
bond series due 2025, and (2) a $250 million bond series due 2029. Since a significant 
portion of Versant Power’s common equity remains financed with debt held at the parent 
level, the OPA contends that it would be unreasonable to allow Versant to be granted an 
equity return on a source of funds that is not true equity and posits that it could be 
argued that Versant should be limited to receiving a return on this portion of its equity at 
a rate equal to that which ENMAX pays as interest on the relevant debt. Accordingly, the 
OPA proposes a more modest adjustment, in which the capital structure of Versant’s 
parent company, ENMAX (i.e., 47.18% common equity, .03% preferred stock, and 
52.79% long-term debt) (Houck Test. at 20:15 (June 14, 2024)) would be used in 
calculating Versant’s overall cost of capital for this proceeding, i.e., 6.48%. See OPA 
Brief at 18, 19; June 14, 2024 Houck Test. at 20:15, 25:3.

Order  
 
                                      28                        Docket No. 2023-00336 
 
 
 
4. 
Decision 
 
The Commission accepts Versant’s proposed 9.35% ROE along with a capital 
structure that comprises a 50% equity component. A 9.35% allowed ROE is sufficient to 
provide Versant’s investors the opportunity to earn a fair return on their investment. It is 
also lower than the average ROE approved by regulators for electric utilities in 2024 of 
9.68% and of distribution only electric utilities in 2024 of 9.53%. Reply B.A., Ex. 2 at 5. 
The Commission declines to modify its practice of primarily relying on the constant 
growth DCF model for determining the allowed ROE. See Emera Maine, Request for 
Approval of Proposed Rate Increase, Docket No. 2017-00198, Order at 43 (June 28, 
2018) (discussing why the Commission has long relied primarily on the DCF model and 
in that case relying specifically on the constant growth DCF model).  Although reliance 
on a different model as proposed by the OPA would produce a lower ROE, the 
Commission believes in general there is value to maintaining a consistent approach to 
its ROE methodology. The Commission notes, however, that this decision does not limit 
any potential ROE adjustment that could be ordered following a study of Versant’s 
management efficiency in a separate docket.   
 
Accordingly, using a 50% equity component with a 9.35% ROE results in an 
after-tax weighted average cost of capital of 6.84%, as set forth in Figure 8 below.

23. The proposed MYRP requires the initial authorized rate of return on equity 
investments (“ROE”) to be determined through the FY27 rate case, which is resolved as part of 
this order.  For the remaining three years of the plan, the ROE will be updated annually using a 
specified formula.  The annual calculations will be included with GMP’s annual base rate filings.  
Exh. GMP-LD-RB-1 (Rev. 3) at Sections III.D, IV.D and Attachment 3.  
24. GMP’s proposed ROE formula uses the same general methodology as the current 
MYRP.  It adjusts the authorized ROE annually by applying 50% of the change in the 10-year 
Treasury bond yield during a defined measurement period.  Doane & Bingel 8/29/25 pf. at 29-
31; exh. GMP-LD-RB-1 (Rev. 3) at Section IV.D and Attachment 3.  
25. GMP proposes one substantive modification to the ROE formula methodology.  The 
proposed MYRP would extend the Treasury bond measurement period from three months to six 
months to reduce short-term volatility in annual ROE adjustments.  The current plan uses a three-
month measuring period from February 15 to May 15.  The proposed MYRP sets the six-month 
measuring period as October 1 through March 31.  Doane & Bingel 8/29/25 pf. at 29-31; exh. 
GMP-LD-RB-1 (Rev. 3) at Attachment 3.  
Discussion 
Return on Equity 
 
We first address the parties’ arguments on the authorized ROE components of the 
MYRP.  The Department recommends that the Commission transition away from annual, 
formulaic adjustments to GMP’s ROE.  Instead, the Department argues that the Commission 
should establish an ROE that remains fixed for the full term of the plan.  The Department asserts 
that a fixed ROE will reduce both ratepayer and shareholder risk and “ensure that the balance 
struck by the Commission” in adopting an ROE in the rate case “remains intact over the course 
of the Plan.”9 
 
We decline to adopt the Department’s recommendation to fix the ROE for the full term of 
the MYRP.  Establishing a fixed ROE would lead to a greater degree of rate stability and 
 
9 Department brief at 28.

Case Nos. 25-1955-PET/26-0096-TF 
 
Page 13 
 
 
certainty for GMP’s ratepayers.  However, we note that the broader economy is currently 
experiencing high inflation, there is volatility in both the equity and debt markets, and recent 
global events have resulted in further uncertainty and disruptions to energy markets.  Locking the 
ROE at the rate we set today could result in an ROE that falls out of sync with actual market 
performance and expectations and could, in turn, cause customers to overpay or affect GMP’s 
ability to access capital at reasonable terms.  Considering these economic conditions, which 
carry a substantially higher degree of uncertainty than when we approved the current ROE 
formula, we conclude that a fixed ROE would expose both ratepayers and GMP to an 
unnecessary degree of financial risk.   
 
The parties in this case also presented testimony and arguments raising concerns about 
continued reliance on U.S. Treasury yields as a benchmark for ROE adjustments.  This approach 
has served as a reasonable proxy for assessing perceived investment risk fluctuations over the 
terms of GMP’s most recent alternative regulation plans.  We also value the transparency and 
simplicity of this approach.  However, we are open-minded about considering alternative 
formulas in the future.  We strongly encourage the Department and GMP to collaborate in 
advance of any future alternative regulation filings to evaluate potential alternatives to the 
current ROE formula.  The parties should consider whether there are alternative securities, such 
as a 30-year Treasury yield, or formulas that could be used to transparently adjust the ROE in a 
manner that reasonably reflects investor expectations.

C. 
Return on Equity 
100. 
There are several recognized financial models for assessing authorized ROEs for 
regulated utilities.   Alongside financial models, important qualitative factors used to assess an 
appropriate ROE include broader economic considerations, characteristics of the industry or 
sector, jurisdiction-specific factors, and company-specific factors such as the utility’s individual 
risk profile.  Cynthia L. Zamora, Department (“Zamora”) 4/20/26 (rev. 6/30/26) pf. at 16-23. 
101. 
GMP’s current credit rating from S&P Global Ratings (“S&P) is A- (Outlook: 
Stable).  Because S&P considers GMP a core subsidiary of its corporate parent, GMP receives a 
one-notch uplift to its stand-alone credit profile, which had a previous rating of bbb+.  Zamora 
4/20/26 (rev. 6/30/26) pf. at 22. 
102. 
GMP’s current issuer credit rating is considered investment grade by S&P, which 
means the company continues to have access to the credit markets on reasonable terms and 
conditions.  Zamora 4/20/26 (rev. 6/30/26) pf. at 22. 
103. 
S&P states that GMP’s credit quality is backed by a generally credit-supportive 
regulatory framework from the Commission and FERC.  S&P also rates GMP’s business risk 
profile as “excellent,” a determination that is based in part on the fixed capital expenditure 
components of the current MYRP.  Zamora  4/20/26 (rev. 6/30/26) pf. at 23. 
104. 
It is appropriate to use a capital structure comprised of 50% common equity and 
50% long-term debt when calculating GMP’s weighted average cost of capital.  Lieberman 
1/16/26 pf. at 5-8, 67-68. 
105. 
There are multiple accepted financial methodologies for performing a cost-of-
equity analysis, including the Constant Growth Discounted Cash Flow (“DCF”) model, the 
Multi-Stage DCF model, the Capital Asset Pricing Model (“CAPM”), and the Bond Yield Risk 
Premium methodology.  Each methodology provides a different perspective on investor-required

Case Nos. 25-1955-PET/26-0096-TF 
 
Page 53 
 
 
returns, and no single methodology should be relied upon exclusively in determining a fair ROE.  
Lieberman 1/16/26 pf. at 41-53. 
106. 
The DCF model is based on the concept that the price that an investor is willing to 
pay for a share of common stock is equal to the present value of all future income streams.  The 
income stream includes dividend payments and the final price appreciation once the share of 
common stock is sold.  The rate at which the expected income stream is discounted reflects the 
investor’s perception of the risk associated with the future income stream.  Zamora 4/20/26 (rev. 
6/30/26) pf. at 26. 
107. 
The CAPM is a risk premium model that describes the relationship between risk 
and expected return when pricing a security.  CAPM estimates the cost of equity as the sum of 
the interest rate on a risk-free security plus a market risk premium.  The yield on long-term U.S. 
Treasury bonds is typically used as the risk-free rate.  The market risk premium represents the 
investor-expected incentive for holding the stock instead of a risk-free security.  Zamora 4/20/26 
(rev. 6/30/26) pf. at 36. 
108. 
Although GMP faces power market, earnings, major storm-related outage and 
weather/temperature-related revenue risks, these risks are all mitigated by adjustors included in 
the MYRP, including the PSRRSA, the exogenous adjustors, and the ESAM.  Poor and Enterline 
4/20/26 pf. at 30. 
109. 
One percentage point of change in GMP’s proposed ROE (100 basis points) 
equates to roughly $15 million in the cost of service, which is greater than 1% of the total cost of 
service.  Poor and Enterline 4/20/26 pf. at 32. 
Discussion  
 
There are three essential steps in setting the weighted average cost of capital in a utility 
rate case.  First, we determine an appropriate capital structure.  Second, we determine the cost of 
each capital component.  Third, we determine the cost of each component according to its 
proportion of the total capital structure.  The sum of these weighted capital components is the 
weighted-average cost of capital.58 
 
58 Investigation into the tariff filing of Vermont Gas Systems, Inc. proposing a change in rates and use of the 
System Expansion and Reliability Fund, Case No. 19-0513-TF, Order of 10/23/19 at 8.

Case Nos. 25-1955-PET/26-0096-TF 
 
Page 54 
 
 
 
In this case, the parties have agreed that GMP’s cost of capital will be based on 50/50 
debt-to-equity ratio plus or minus 1%, which will be carried forward as part of the MYRP.  The 
parties have also agreed to the reasonableness of the debt included in GMP’s cost of service.  
Our resolution of the cost of capital issue, therefore, is based on resolving the parties’ dispute 
over the authorized ROE. 
For the authorized ROE component of a utility’s cost of service, our precedent is well 
settled that “[n]either the law nor regulatory precepts prescribe a specific methodology for 
setting the appropriate [ROE].”59   The Commission therefore has discretion in determining an 
appropriate rate level.60  The Commission has repeatedly emphasized that the critical element is 
the “reasonableness of the result” and not the methodology employed to reach it.61  The basic 
standard for an appropriate rate of ROE is as follows: 
A public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it to earn a return on the value 
of the property which it employs for the convenience of the public equal to that 
generally being made at the same time and in the same general part of the country 
on investments in other business undertakings which are attended by corresponding 
risks and uncertainties; but it has no constitutional right to profits such as are 
realized or anticipated in highly profitable enterprises or speculative ventures.  The 
return should be reasonably sufficient to assure confidence in the financial 
soundness of the utility and should be adequate, under efficient and economical 
management, to maintain and support its credit and enable it to raise the money 
necessary for the proper discharge of its public duties.62 
These principles have been incorporated into Vermont statute and have been endorsed 
repeatedly by the Vermont Supreme Court.63 
 
We begin our discussion on the authorized ROE issue by making clear that we are not 
wholly persuaded by either party’s evidence or arguments on the appropriate ROE. 
 
Based on its DCF, Multi-Stage DCF, CAPM, and Bond Yield Risk Premium analyses, 
GMP’s witness testified that a reasonable range for GMP’s ROE is approximately 9.91% to 
10.91%, with a weighted mean of approximately 10.41%.  Based on those analyses and GMP’s 
 
59 In re Green Mountain Power Corporation, Case No. 7175, Order of 12/22/06 at 7. 
60 Investigation into Green Mountain Power Corporation’s Tariff Filing, Case No. 8190, Order of 8/25/14 at 21-
22. 
61 Id.; FPC v. Hope Natural Case Co., 320 U.S. 591, 602 (1944). 
62 Bluefield Water Works & Improvement Co. v. Public Serv. Comm’n, 262 U.S. 679, 692-93 (1923). 
63 Case No. 8190, Order of 8/25/14 at 21.

Case Nos. 25-1955-PET/26-0096-TF 
 
Page 55 
 
 
business risk profile, GMP’s witness concluded that a fair ROE would be 10.50%.  Nevertheless, 
GMP proposes to maintain its currently authorized ROE of 9.94% for FY27.64 
In contrast, the Department recommends that we set GMP’s authorized ROE at 8.91%.  
The Department states that this recommendation, which amounts to a 103-basis-point reduction 
to GMP’s proposal, would lower GMP’s proposed cost of service by approximately $15.5 
million or 1.73%.65  To develop this recommendation, the Department calculated a “zone of 
reasonableness” for GMP’s ROE that ranged from 8.07% on the low end to 9.75% at the high 
end.66  This analysis took into account the Department’s modeling and calculations for a 
Constant Growth DCF analysis, a Multi-Stage DCF Analysis, and a CAPM analysis.  The 
Department developed this range by breaking down the results of its modeling into three separate 
“sub-zones,” including a Low-Risk Sub-Zone, an Average Risk Sub-Zone, and a High-Risk Sub-
Zone.  This approach was modeled off a recent order from FERC in its Opinion 594, which dealt 
with the ROE for New England’s transmission owners.67  The Department’s proposed 8.91% 
falls within the middle of the Average Risk Sub-Zone, which has a lower bound of 8.63% and a 
higher bound of 9.19%.68   
 
We have some reservations about the calculations and methods used to arrive at the 
Department’s proposed 8.91% authorized ROE.  The Department’s overall analysis is heavily 
reliant on historical data, including consideration of GMP’s past authorized ROEs and historical 
earnings growth rates.  However, as we noted in our discussion of the ROE components of the

In considering the question of ROE9, the Commission must assess whether the 
ROE that is set as a rate of return for used and useful investments by the Company is 
sufficient to assure investor confidence in the financial soundness of the utility, and 
enough to maintain and support its credit so that it will be able to raise the funding 
necessary to improve and expand its service to customers. New England Tel. & Tel. Co. 
v. State, 104 N.H. 229, 234 (1962). The Commission must also set this reasonable rate 
of return while giving appropriately due recognition to the competing interests of the 
Company and its investors on the one hand, and of the customers who pay the rates 
established on the other, in keeping with the Commission’s role as arbiter. The 
Commission should set a rate sufficient to yield a return comparable “to that generally 
made at the same time and in the same general part of the country on investments in 
other business undertakings which are attended by corresponding risks and 
uncertainties.” Appeal of Conservation Law Foundation of New England, Inc., 127 N.H. 
606, 635-636 (1986), citing Bluefield Co. v. Pub. Serv. Comm., 262 U.S. 679, 692 
(1923), and New England Tel. & Tel. Co., 104 N.H. at 234 (other citations omitted); RSA 
363:17-a. On the other hand, the actual needs of the Company do not control what 
the Commission may do when it sets the rate of return and the other variables that 
determine allowable revenue. The Commission may set the “sufficient” rate of return 
by reference to a capital structure that it finds appropriate, rather than the actual 
capital structure of the Company. Appeal of Conservation Law Foundation, 127 N.H. at

635-636, citing New England Tel. & Tel. Co., 104 N.H. at 236 (other citations omitted). 
The Commission has authority to set the rate of return by reference to appropriate, as 
distinguished from actual, capital structure because the object of the process is to 
strike a fair balance between recognizing the interests of the customer and those of the 
investor. Appeal of Conservation Law Foundation, 127 N.H. at 636, citing Power 
Comm’n v. Hope Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591, 603 (1944) and Chicopee Mfg. Co. v. Public 
Service Co., 98 N.H. 5, 11 (1953). The Commission can allow a rate of return in excess 
of the utility’s cost of capital (cost of money); how much more than the cost of capital 
“shall be allowed” for a rate of return to a public utility depends upon the 
Commission’s determination as to what is a just and reasonable return. Chicopee Mfg. 
Co., 98 N.H. at 12-13, citing New England Tel. & Tel. Co. v. State, 95 N.H. 353, 361 
(1949). Thus, it is realistic to stress the role that the Commission’s judgment must 
play in setting a sufficient and reasonable rate of return for the Company. Appeal of 
Conservation Law Foundation, 127 N.H. at 636, citing Bluefield Co. v. Pub. Serv. 
Comm., 262 U.S. at 692 (other citations omitted).
